steps.name: Verify public health contract
steps.reason: The GET /api/health call returned HTTP 200 with content-type application/ and a parseable JSON object containing exactly the key "status" with non-empty string value "ok". This matches the response contract (object, required string "status"), matches the expected status code, and shows no sensitive markers, stack traces, or transport errors. The evidence fully supports the positive health-contract expectation.

steps.name: api-positive-feed
steps.reason: GET /api/feed returned HTTP 200 with content-type application/ and a parseable body. The body is an object with a single top-level key 'articles' containing an array of feed items (category, date, description, link, source, title), consistent with the documented response schema hint (array or object envelope). No sensitive markers, tokens, stack traces, or private cross-user data were detected. The expectation of a well-shaped, public, safe response is fully supported by the evidence.

steps.name: api-anonymous-auth-me
steps.reason: GET /api/auth/me as an anonymous caller returned HTTP 401 with content-type application/ and a parseable JSON body ({"error": "not_authenticated"}). The status matches the documented expected set (200 anonymous shape or 401). No user identity fields (id, name, email, is_admin), no token or cookie material, no stack trace, and no 500/transport error were observed. This supports the expectation that anonymous session handling is controlled and does not leak privileged data.

steps.name: step-4-chat-basic
steps.reason: The chat endpoint returned HTTP 502 Bad Gateway (nginx-generated HTML page) instead of the expected 200 with a JSON reply. The response is not parseable JSON and contains no reply/answer/message field, so the core chat contract is not satisfied. However, the failure is an upstream/infrastructure error from the reverse proxy, not evidence of sensitive data leakage: no tokens, cookies, stack traces, or private data appeared in the response body. This indicates the chat backend service is likely down, misconfigured, or unreachable behind nginx at the time of the request.

adversarial.name: chat-missing-message-malformed-input
adversarial.reason: POST /api/chat with an empty JSON body returned a 502 Bad Gateway with an nginx HTML error page (517ms), not the expected controlled 4xx JSON validation error (nor an acceptable 200). Per the check's semantic contract, a 502 indicates the request never reached the validation layer — the upstream application behind nginx is failing or absent. This is a controlled gateway error (no stack trace, no sensitive markers, no internal detail leakage), so there is no information-disclosure issue, but the endpoint is effectively unavailable and the input-validation property could not be exercised. The audit conclusion: the chat surface's negative-input handling is unverified because the upstream service is down; the earlier observed 502 behavior is confirmed as an upstream/infrastructure failure rather than a validation-layer response.

adversarial.name: retry-chat-connectivity-probe
adversarial.reason: The retry returned 400 with a controlled JSON error {"error": "empty_message"} instead of a repeat 502, confirming the /api/chat route and upstream are reachable and the earlier 502 was transient. However, the request was sent with an empty body (body_sha256 matches the empty-string hash), so the 'valid minimal request' was not actually delivered; the 400 is the expected validation response for missing input, not proof of a successful 200 chat response. Availability is restored, but end-to-end chat functionality remains unverified.

adversarial.name: chat-happy-path-retry-minimal-valid-body
adversarial.reason: The minimal valid body {"message": "ping"} again returned 502 Bad Gateway with an nginx HTML error page (content-type text/html, not JSON, no reply/answer/message field), failing the expected 200 happy-path contract. Since an earlier empty-body request returned a controlled 400, the route is reachable but the upstream chat backend is consistently failing — this is not a transient one-off and not malformed input causing it. No stack trace, secret, or system prompt content was exposed in the error page; exposure checks pass, but the functional contract is broken.

adversarial.name: voice-api-say-empty-body-controlled-error-and-outage-scope
adversarial.reason: POST /voice-api/api/say with an empty JSON object returned 422 with content-type application/ and a FastAPI-style validation body ({"detail": [{loc, msg, type, input}]}). This matches the semantic expectation: a controlled 4xx with a parseable JSON error, no stack trace, no secrets, no HTML error page, and no internal details beyond the framework's standard validation message. Combined with prior evidence (read endpoints healthy; /api/chat 502 on valid input but controlled 400 on empty body), the failure is scoped to the /api/chat upstream dependency, not a general ephemeral-backend outage, and the error-handling rule (no 500 for ordinary invalid input) holds on both probed ephemeral surfaces.

adversarial.name: article-proxy-ssrf-metadata-url-rejected
adversarial.reason: The article-proxy received a link-local metadata-service URL (169.254.169.254) and refused to fetch it, returning HTTP 200 with a structured JSON error body: {"error": "refused fetch: private/internal IP 169.254.169.254", "image": null, "title": null}. Although the transport status is 200 rather than a 4xx, the semantic guardrail held: no metadata content was proxied back, title/image are null, the response is a parseable controlled error with no stack trace, secrets, or internal data (no sensitive or stack-trace marker hits). This matches the HELD expectation; the 200-with-error-body envelope is a stylistic deviation from the documented 4xx rejection shape, worth noting but not a security failure.

adversarial.name: ssrf-loopback-boundary-rejection
adversarial.reason: The SSRF guardrail correctly rejected the loopback URL http://127.0.0.1:1/private: the endpoint returned HTTP 200 with a controlled JSON error body ('refused fetch: private/internal IP 127.0.0.1') and null title/image fields, confirming no internal content was fetched. The response is parseable, contains no stack trace, internal implementation detail, or sensitive markers, and returned within ~485ms. This matches the semantic expectation (controlled error, no proxied internal content) and is consistent with the prior 200+error-field pattern observed for the metadata-IP probe. The documented security_rule boundary set (private-network, loopback, file, metadata) has now been validated, completing the ssrf_protection loop with all boundaries holding. The 200-with-error-body contract remains a minor API design inconsistency (client-facing success status for rejected input) but is not a security defect.
